paragraphs: Swamiji noticed a habit we all share: we assume our own little mental world is the whole world, and that our ideas of right, duty and usefulness are the only ones worth having.

On one trip to Europe, his ship passed through Marseilles, where a bull-fight was taking place. The English passengers on board were furious, condemning the whole thing as cruel. A little later, in England, he heard about a group of English prize-fighters who had gone to Paris and been thrown out without ceremony by the French, who found boxing brutal.

Seeing the same pattern in country after country, Swamiji said he began to understand Christ's advice not to judge others. The more we learn, the more we discover how little we know, and how many-sided the human mind is.

He admitted something about himself too. As a boy he used to criticise the harsh ascetic practices of his countrymen. Great preachers had criticised them, even the Buddha. But as he grew older he felt he had no right to judge. He sometimes wished he had even a small share of those ascetics' power to act and endure. Often, he confessed, his criticism did not really come from disliking self-torture at all, but from plain cowardice, because he could not do it himself.
learn: Before mocking someone else's customs or choices, ask whether you're judging from wisdom or just from habit, or even from envy of what you can't do. Humility is a sign of real learning.
